newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Excess funds flood Pakistani interbank market.
newsitem.headline: Excess funds flood Pakistani interbank market.

text.p: Overnight rates hit rock bottom as an estimated 11 billion rupees ($272 million) in excess funds flooded the Pakistani interbank market, dealers said on Tuesday.
Overnights were traded at one to two percent on Monday as the market remained inundated with liquidity, Farhan Moin, a senior dealer at Standard Chartered Bank, said.
He said the surplus was partly the result of inflows from maturing open market operations (OMO) conducted by the State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP).

Moin also cited an SBP move to cut the statutory liquidity requirement of banks to 20 percent from 25 percent with effect from May 28 as part of a strategy to release funds for the private sector and put downward pressure on interest rates.
"The SBP decision is likely to gradually inject 46 billion rupees into the market," Moin said.

An analyst at brokerage house KASB & Co said: "Previously the banks were required to keep 25 percent of their total time and demand liabilities in government securities, along with a five percent statutory cash reserve, with the SBP."
"We feel that this move is a step towards a liberal monetary policy aimed at expanding the private sector credit limit by 82 billion rupees," the analyst said.
He said it could eventually pump about 45 billion rupees of extra liquidity into the market, but the full effect would be delayed until government securities mature or are retired.
Moin said the market would stay in surplus despite a central bank announcement that it planned to soak up three billion rupees in an auction of short-term federal bonds on Tuesday.
He said the SBP's weekly OMO on Wednesday would be crucial in determining the cut-off yield, which has fallen sharply in the past few open market operations.

The excess liquidity prompted the SBP to mop up 7.325 billion rupees cheaply last week, as cut-off rates gradually fell to 16.7 percent in the last OMO from 17.5 percent. Moin said the rate might drop as low as 16.5 percent on Wednesday.
He said the excess liquidity was expected to pull down interest rates which would help corporate clients.
On Wednesday, the SBP capped government borrowing for budget support at 58 billion rupees for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June).
The credit plan for 1997/98 aims to curb monetary expansion to about 14 percent and to hold public borrowing from the SBP to 30 billion rupees and from commercial banks to 28 billion.
The SBP has also approved a credit limit of 82 billion rupees for the private sector in 1997/98 in a bid to promote an industrial revival and expand trade.
